To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
recipients' gratitude is influenced not only by the perceived intentions of their helpers but also by their normative expectations about what a fair helper'should' do.

(1) recipients' gratitude towards unconditional offers was greater than towards conditional ones, and (2) this gratitude was linked to a greater eagerness to reciprocate, and (3) this eagerness to recipocate was linked to a higher rate of reciprocation.

when recipients lack the information to infer the intentions of the potential helpers, they use normative beliefs about what a 'fair' individual should do to guide their behaviour and, as a consequence, reciprocate more.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how people react to the receipt of a 'gift' when they are unaware of the donor's intentions.
the role of perceived fairness in cooperative interactions, and how it influences people's affective reactions and subsequent behaviours in a double anonymous game.
the question of whether and when people use 'normative beliefs' about fairness to infer the intentions of others.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the perceived intentions of donors, as well as the perceived fairness of their behaviour, influence recipients' gratitude and their subsequent behaviour.
recipients' gratitude is not only triggered by the perception that the help is given for free, but also by the perception that it is given in a helpful manner.
the injunctive norm of reciprocity can be a powerful guide for recipients' reactions to a gift, even in the absence of information on the donor's intention.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the perceived intention of the donor, rather than the normative belief of fairness, plays a key role in determining the recipient's affective and behavioural responses to the help.
the perceived intention of a donor, rather than the normative belief of fairness, would be the main determinant of recipients' reactions.
recipients of a gift, in the absence of information about the donor's intentions, use normative beliefs about fairness to infer the donor's intentions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
people are not only sensitive to the fairness of a behaviour, they are also sensitive to the intentions of the person performing it. When people have no information to infer intentions
people are able to make fair inferences about others even when they are not in a position to observe the others' behaviours.
the perceived fairness of a behaviour can be influenced by normative beliefs about the fairness of the behaviour, irrespective of whether the behaviour was intended to be fair or unfair.
